blocks.text: To give the potential at a point a value, we need a reference point that is assigned zero potential; this is usually taken at infinity. If A is at infinity with VA = 0, the potential at B is VB = W/qo, or simply V = W/qo (16.6).

blocks.title: Electric potential
blocks.text: The electric potential at any point in an electric field is the work done in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to that point, keeping it in electrostatic equilibrium. Potential and potential difference are both scalar quantities, because work and charge are scalars.
Potential due to a point charge

The field of a point charge q is radial (Fig 16.2) and varies as 1/r^2, so dV = -E dr cannot be used directly over a long distance. Take two points A and B very close together, at distances rA and rB from q, so that E is almost constant between them: rB = rA + dr (16.7). The field at their midpoint r is E = (1/4 pi eo) q / r^2 (16.10); since the points are very close, the arithmetic mean of rA and rB can be taken equal to the geometric mean, so r^2 = rA rB (16.11) and E = (1/4 pi eo) q / (rA rB) (16.12).

The work done in moving a unit positive charge from B to A equals the potential difference: VA - VB = E (rB - rA) (16.13). Substituting E gives VA - VB = (1/4 pi eo) q (rB - rA)/(rA rB) = (1/4 pi eo) q (1/rA - 1/rB) (16.15). This holds for any two points, because a long path can be built from many short steps whose terms cancel in pairs. Taking B at infinity (VB = 0, 1/rB = 0) gives VA = (1/4 pi eo) q / rA (16.16), and in general the potential at distance r from q is V = (1/4 pi eo) q / r (16.17).
The potential is negative if q is negative. With several charges, each contributes to the potential, and the total potential at a point is the algebraic sum of the individual potentials.

blocks.alt: Left: two horizontal plates, positive on top and negative below, with vertical field arrows E pointing down; a positive test charge between points A (lower) and B (upper) has a green arrow pointing up, against the field. Right: a positive point charge +q with field lines radiating outward and two nearby points A and B on one line, a small distance dr apart.
blocks.caption: Potential difference in a uniform field, and the radial field of a point charge (original diagram after Figs 16.1 and 16.2).
blocks.long_description: In a uniform field the potential changes steadily (E = V/d). Near a point charge the field gets weaker with distance, so the potential is found by adding the work over many small steps, giving V = kq/r.

blocks.text: Find the potential at a point 1.2 m from a charge of 5.0 x 10^-8 C. Solution: V = (1/4 pi eo) q / r = (9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2)(5.0 x 10^-8 C) / 1.2 m = 375 V.

Charges of +8 uC and -4 uC are 60 cm apart (Fig 16.3). Where on the line through them is the potential zero? Solution: the potential is zero where the positive and negative contributions are equal in size. Because the positive charge is larger, both zero points lie closer to the smaller negative charge: one between the charges (A) and one beyond the negative charge (B). At A, a distance x from the positive charge: k(8 uC)/x = k(4 uC)/(60 cm - x), so 8(60 - x) = 4x, 480 - 8x = 4x, and x = 40 cm. At B, a distance y beyond the negative charge: k(8 uC)/(60 cm + y) = k(4 uC)/y, so 8y = 4(60 + y), 4y = 240 cm, and y = 60 cm.

blocks.title: The working for point B
blocks.text: In the book, the expressions written for the potentials at B repeat those for A (with x and 60 cm - x); the balance condition used, 4(60 cm + y) = 8y, is the correct one for B, as shown above.

blocks.alt: Top: a line with +8 uC on the left and -4 uC 60 cm to its right; point A is 40 cm from the positive charge, between them, and point B is 60 cm beyond the negative charge. Bottom: a sketch of the potential along the line; it is large and positive near +8 uC, crosses zero at A, becomes large and negative near -4 uC, and rises back to cross zero at B before approaching zero far away.
blocks.caption: Zero-potential points for two charges (original diagram for Example 16.3).
blocks.long_description: Potential is a scalar, so the two contributions simply add with their signs. Zero points lie where the larger positive charge is further away, so that its bigger charge is balanced by greater distance.

blocks.prompt: Is the potential zero anywhere on the left of the +8 uC charge in Example 16.3? Explain.
blocks.explanation: No. To the left, every point is closer to the larger +8 uC charge than to the -4 uC charge, so the positive contribution is always bigger and V is never zero (except far away, where it tends to zero).

items: V = W/qo with zero at infinity; potential is a scalar.
Point charge: V = (1/4 pi eo) q / r; negative for negative q.
Several charges: add the potentials algebraically.
